In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the prognosis of patients who have undergone breast-conserving surgery for primary breast cancer is influenced little, if at all, by the development of local recurrence in the treated breast, provided that the recurrence is operable.

salvage surgery is indicated for all patients in whom the disease is operable, that the type of operation used is of secondary importance, that total mastectomy is probably preferred for most patients, and that wide excision is indicated for a small minority.

the use of a wide excision for a small, well-cirs-cumscribed, favorable recurrence has been reported by our group ( 6 ), and is apparently used in other centers ( 1, 2 ) although other published reports have not yet been reported.

the results of salvage mastectomy after breast-conserving treatment are not significantly different from those obtained after salvage surgery for local recurrence after mastectomy, provided the latter is performed with adequate margins.
local failure is uncommon (less than 5% at 10 years), and is associated with a 50% 5-year survival rate, provided that the recurrence is operable (i.e., not involving skin, chest wall or axilla).
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to be more aggressive about screening for breast cancer.
there are many different factors that can influence the risk of recurrence, and the risk of recurrence can be quite high for some patients.
we have to do a better job of educating our patients about their options and helping them to make decisions that are best for them.
